subtype: Parent unsure whether to push or protect [Receiver]
passage: Vishal, you're asking whether to keep Nishant home from the school trip. Let me tell you what I did with you. At nine you were scared of swimming lessons. First I shouted, "Just jump in," and pushed you to the edge. You shook so hard you were sick. So then I stopped the lessons completely. No pool, no worry. But your fear only grew; soon you wouldn't even walk past the pool. Your Amma said, "Neither way is working, Madhav." So we tried small steps. One day, only sitting by the pool. Then feet in the water. Then the shallow end, me beside you, saying, "You're scared, and you're doing it." It took the whole summer. By Diwali you swam a length and grinned at me.

qa.q: What was Vishal scared of at nine?
qa.a: Vishal was scared of swimming lessons.

qa.q: What did Madhav want when the lessons were stopped completely?
qa.a: Madhav wanted to shield Vishal from worry after the pushing went badly; the feeling behind it was an anxious protectiveness.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Madhav's story?
qa.a: When Amma said neither way was working, Madhav switched to small steps with warm encouragement beside the pool.

qa.q: How did young Vishal experience the small steps compared with being pushed?
qa.a: Being pushed made Vishal shake and be sick, while small steps with Madhav alongside let Vishal face the pool and finally grin after swimming a length.

grounding: A parent swings between forcing bravery and removing the fear, then finds that small steady steps with warm encouragement work.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the lane, and the annual-day rehearsal in Margao started in twenty minutes. Francis, eight, sat on the stairs with his raincoat half on. "I'm not going on stage. My stomach's all funny."
Vidya felt the old pull both ways: to say, "Enough, get in the car," or to keep him home. She had tried both. Forcing had ended in tears at the gate; staying home had made the next day worse.
She knelt on the wet step. "You don't have to sing the solo today. Can you just stand in the back row of the choir? I'll wait at the door where you can see me."
"Only the back row?"
"Only the back row. That's brave enough for today."

qa.q: Where did Vidya offer to wait?
qa.a: At the door, where Francis could see her.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as Francis sat on the stairs?
qa.a: Vidya felt torn and stressed, pulled between forcing him to go and keeping him home, with the rehearsal only twenty minutes away.

qa.q: Which choice did Vidya make, and why is it wiser than her old ones?
qa.a: Vidya offered a smaller step, the back row with her in sight, which avoids both pressure and avoidance.

qa.q: How might Francis feel about a back-row-only plan?
qa.a: Francis might still feel nervous, but relieved that the task is small enough to try with his mother in view.

grounding: A parent of an anxious child is torn between forcing and rescuing, and chooses a small step with warm support instead.

passage: It was the last day to sign up for the school trip, and it was pouring. Ojas, nine, stood in the doorway, refusing to walk to the bus stop, where a big dog always sat under the shelter. Ankita had tried both ways already. Last month she'd said, 'Just walk past it, don't be silly,' and Ojas had cried all the way. Then for three weeks she had driven him everywhere. Ojas had got more scared, not less. Today she crouched. 'Let's do just one step. We'll walk to the corner, look at the shelter from there, and then I'll drive you.' Ojas held her hand tight. At the corner he looked, breathing fast. 'Good,' she said warmly. 'Tomorrow we'll try the next lamppost.' He signed up for the trip in the car.

qa.q: Where did the big dog always sit?
qa.a: Under the shelter at the bus stop.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when his mother told him not to be silly?
qa.a: He felt frightened and pushed, and cried the whole way.

qa.q: What approach did Ankita choose today, and why is it better?
qa.a: One small step, to the corner to look, with warm praise, then the next lamppost tomorrow; it builds courage without forcing or avoiding.

qa.q: How might three weeks of being driven have affected Ojas?
qa.a: It kept him away from the fear, so the fear grew, and he got more scared rather than less.

grounding: Shows a child affected by a parent swinging between forcing bravery and removing the difficulty, and the change when she offers small steady steps with warmth.

passage: Vishal's father had decided on Sunday that he would 'cure' the fear of water. At the Nagpur municipal pool, Ramesh lifted his ten-year-old and dropped him in the shallow end. Vishal came up spluttering and screaming. On the auto ride home Ramesh, shaken, promised he would never have to swim again. For a month Vishal skipped every class trip near water, and Ramesh felt relieved, then uneasy. Now Vishal would not even splash in the bucket bath. Ramesh talked to the swimming coach. The next Sunday they sat together on the pool steps, feet in. 'Just this today,' Ramesh said. The Sunday after, knees. Vishal gripped the rail, looked at his father and said, 'Maybe waist next week?' Ramesh squeezed his shoulder. 'Only if you want, beta. I'm proud of you.'

qa.q: Where did Ramesh drop Vishal in?
qa.a: The shallow end of the Nagpur municipal pool.

qa.q: How was Vishal feeling when he came up spluttering?
qa.a: He was terrified and shocked, screaming after being dropped in without warning.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Ramesh swung from forcing Vishal in to banning water completely; small steady steps on the pool steps, with warmth, fixed it.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel during the month of avoidance?
qa.a: He felt relieved at first, then uneasy when Vishal would not even splash in the bucket bath.

grounding: Shows a child caught between a parent's forcing and over-protecting, and the progress that comes from small warm steps instead.

passage:
'Salma, the party's at four. Get your shoes on.'
'I don't want to go, Ammi.'
'Last time you said that, I let you stay home. And the time before.'
'My tummy feels funny.'
Charu sat on the bed. 'I know parties feel big to you. I've been doing two wrong things, I think. Sometimes I push, sometimes I just let you hide. Neither helps, does it?'
Salma picked at her sock. 'When you push, I cry. When I stay home, I feel sad later.'
'So how about a middle way? We go for twenty minutes. You give Meher her present, I stay nearby, and then you choose: stay or leave.'
'You won't go away?'
'I'll be right by the gate.'
Salma thought. 'Twenty minutes. And you'll hold my hand in.'
'Deal.'

qa.q: How long did Charu suggest they stay at the party?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How does Salma feel about both pushing and staying home?
qa.a: When pushed she is scared and cries, and when allowed to stay home she feels sad later, so she is torn.

qa.q: What makes Charu's middle way a wise choice?
qa.a: It is a small, clear step with Charu nearby and a choice at the end, so Salma builds courage without being forced or avoiding.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu to admit her two wrong ways?
qa.a: It may feel uncomfortable, but it lets her work with Salma instead of swinging back and forth.

grounding: Shows a child affected by a parent's swings between pushing and letting her avoid, and a middle way of small steps with warm encouragement.

subtype: Parent unsure whether to push or protect [Receiver]
passage: When my son Ojas started refusing swimming lessons, I didn't know what to do. Some days I dragged him to the pool while he cried at the edge, and felt like a monster. Other days I let him skip, and he'd look relieved, then be even more scared the next week. My wife said, 'Nilesh, you swing between pushing and rescuing.' She was right. The coach suggested something in between. In the first week, Ojas just sat on the steps with his feet in. In the second, he stood in the shallow end holding the rail. I stayed on the bench each time, cheering small things. Last Saturday he let go of the rail for five seconds and grinned at me. I nearly cried.

qa.q: Where did Ojas sit in the first week?
qa.a: On the steps with his feet in.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when dragging Ojas to the pool?
qa.a: Nilesh felt guilty, like a monster, watching Ojas cry at the edge.

qa.q: What approach finally helped Ojas?
qa.a: Small steady steps, feet in, then standing holding the rail, with warm encouragement from the bench.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when he let go of the rail?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, grinning after managing five seconds.

grounding: A parent of an anxious child swings between forcing and rescuing, then finds small steady steps with warm encouragement.
